blocks.text: [III, 345] It is asked why the Egyptians are compared with flies in these words, Es. VII, 18. The Lord shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt; and different authors offer different answers. Jerome: He calls the Egyptians flies because of the filth of idolatry and because they are an unwarlike people. Basil thinks the reference is to τὸ εὐτελὲς τῶν ἀντικειμένων δυνάδυνάμεων· [III, 346] μυῖα γάρ ἐστι ζῶον ἀπὸ κόπρου τὴν γένεσιν ἔχον, ὀχληρὸν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις γένος, καὶ μυσαρὸν ὂν, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ὀχληρὰ, καὶ ὁ θάνατος βδελυκτὸς [to euteles tōn antikeimenōn dynadynameōn; myia gar esti zōon apo koprou tēn genesin echon, ochlēron tois anthrōpois genos, kai mysaron on, kai hē zōē ochlēra, kai ho thanatos bdelyktos], the worthlessness of the forces that are set against the Israelites; for the fly is generated from dung, and is a kind hostile to men and abominable, whose life is troublesome and whose death is execrable. But Cyril asserts that the Egyptians are compared with flies διά τοι τὸ πλῆθος, καὶ τὸ μὴ λίαν εὔηχες τῆς φωνῆς [dia toi to plēthos, kai to mē lian euēches tēs phōnēs], because of their multitude and their discordant and uncouth speech, as though it were not so much speech as the buzzing of flies. The simplest course seems to be to refer it to their multitude, with the Chaldee [col. 499] translator, whose paraphrase reads thus: יכלי יי לעם קטרי משרית גבריא דסגיאין כרבביא וייתינון מארעא דמצרים, The Lord shall call to the people of the bands of an army of strong men (that is, in which forces of strong men are joined together and sworn together), who are many as flies, and he shall bring them from the land of Egypt. R. Selomo too understands here חילות רבות כזבובים, an army as numerous as flies. And Abarbanel: המשיל אותם בזבוב לקלות מרוצתם ולרוב האספם, He compares them with flies because of the swiftness of their course and because of the multitude of their gathering. Of these, the former comes from Kimchi, the latter from the Chaldee and Solomon. I think the latter is to be preferred, because Egypt was once populous beyond belief. Herodotus, book 2, chapters 60 and 177, relates that seven hundred thousand people gathered at Bubastis for the festival of Diana, and that under Amasis twenty thousand cities in Egypt were inhabited. In the kingdom of Ptolemy Philadelphus, of which Egypt was the greatest part, Theocritus in Idyll 17 counts more than thirty-three thousand towns. Rightly, then, are the Egyptians compared with flies, whose multitude is immense. Hence Plautus in the Truculentus, Act 1, Scene 1:
For now there are almost more pimps and harlots than there once were flies, when the heat is at its greatest.
And Homer, Iliad β', line 469, says that the forces of the Greeks stood in great number on the Scamandrian meadow,
Ἠΰτε μυιάων ἁδινάων ἔθνεα πολλὰ [Ēute myiaōn hadinaōn ethnea polla], Like the very many tribes of thronging flies.
